title: Knight's Reachable Region (Graph DFS)
real_world_story: A board game engine highlights every square a knight can reach before the player commits a move. The board contains blocked squares, so the engine must follow the jumps from square to square instead of assuming the whole board is open.

real_world_connection.input_represents: Board grid where '.' is a free square and 'X' is a blocked square
real_world_connection.query_represents: The square where the knight currently stands
real_world_connection.algorithm_represents: Following knight jumps from square to square and marking every square that can be reached

problem_statement: Given an R x C board of '.' (free) and 'X' (blocked) and a free starting square (sr, sc), count every free square a knight can reach from the start using any number of knight moves. A knight moves two squares in one direction and one square in the other, in all eight combinations, and it may not land on a blocked square or leave the board. The starting square counts as reachable.
task: Return the number of free squares reachable from (sr, sc), including the starting square itself.
input_format: The first line contains two integers R and C. The next R lines each contain C characters ('.' or 'X'). The final line contains two integers sr sc.
output_format: Print the number of reachable free squares, including the starting square.
constraints: Board cells are free (.) or blocked (X)
The starting square is always free

examples.explanation: From (0,0) the knight can reach 8 of the 9 squares. The centre square (1,1) can never be reached, because no knight jump ends there on a 3 x 3 board.

expected_algorithm.name: Graph DFS
expected_algorithm.reason: Every square is a vertex and every legal knight jump is an edge, so a depth-first traversal from the start marks exactly the connected region of the board graph the knight can move in.

complexity.time: O(R * C) because each square is visited once and has eight neighbours
complexity.space: O(R * C) for the visited marks and the stack

hint: Treat every square as a graph vertex and every knight jump as an edge.
Push neighbouring squares onto a stack and mark a square visited when you push it, not when you pop it.
Count each square the first and only time it is removed from the stack.
real_world_takeaway: A depth-first traversal of the board graph answers 'which squares can this piece reach?' in a single pass, even when blocked squares break the board into regions.
